title: Forming participles using naka-
summary: Naka- + a noun or verb root describes how someone is: nakaupô (seated), nakatayô (standing), nakasapatos (in shoes), nakakotse (in a car)
goals: Understand the difference between a gerund and a participle
Form participles with naka- + root word
Use naka- words to describe a state, condition or appearance
Tell a naka- participle apart from the past tense of a maka- verb

blocks.t: Both the English **gerund** and the **participle** are made from verbs, but they do different jobs. In Lesson 38 you saw that a gerund works like a **noun**. A **participle** works like an **adjective**: it describes a noun or pronoun.

blocks.title: Participles in English
items: **Past** participles end in **-ed**, **-n** or **-t**: *the child is **seated***.

blocks.t: In Tagalog, a participle is formed by adding the prefix **naka-** to a **root word**. The root can be a **noun** or a **verb**.

blocks.title: What a naka- word does
items: It expresses the **state, condition or appearance** of a person or thing, based on the root.
It has **no tense forms**: it is descriptive, just like an adjective.

blocks.t: Read each sentence and find the **naka-** word. The English for it is shown in brackets.

items.tl: Ang batà ay nakaupô sa mataás na sílya.
items.en: The child is seated on a high chair. (nakaupô = is seated)

items.tl: Nakatayô sa tabí ng pintô ang áking iná.
items.en: My mother is standing by the door. (nakatayô = is standing)
The man lying down is lazy. (nakahigâ = lying down)
That man with eyeglasses is blind. (nakasalamíng = with eyeglasses)

items.tl: Kailángang nakasapatos ang batà sa paglalarô.
items.en: Children need to be in shoes on when playing. (nakasapatos = to be in shoes)
They were in a car when they arrived. (nakakotse = in a car)

items.tl: Nakatulalâ si Miriam nang dumatíng akó.
items.en: Miriam is in shock when I arrived. (nakatulalâ = in shock)

items.tl: Puwéde ka sumama pero dápat nakamaóng ka.
items.en: You may come along but you should be in jeans. (nakamaóng = in jeans)

blocks.title: Spot the gerund
blocks.t: In *Kailángang nakasapatos ang batà sa **paglalarô***, the last word is a gerund from Lesson 38 (maglarô → paglalarô, playing). The naka- word describes the child; the gerund names the activity.

blocks.title: No tense
blocks.t: Notice that the same naka- word fits *is* (nakaupô: the child **is** seated) and *were* (nakakotse: they **were** in a car). The naka- word itself never changes for tense.

Do not confuse the participle prefix naka- with the **past tense of a maka- verb** (Lesson 18). Maka- verbs show the **capability to do something** (to be able to), and they are purely **action** words.

head: Naka- participle
Past tense of a maka- verb
rows: a describing word, like an adjective
that someone was able to do something
Ang laláking **nakahigâ** ay tamád. (The man lying down is lazy.)
**Nakatúlog** kagabi ang maysakít. (The sick person was able to sleep last night. Lesson 18)
blocks.title: Two kinds of naka- words

blocks.t: The book's exercise asks you to translate these sentences into English to find out whether each naka- word is a **participle** or a **maka- verb** in the past tense. Ask yourself: does it **describe** someone, or say what someone **was able to do**?

head: Sentence
rows: Nakabása na siyá ng mga aklát ni Romulo.
Nakatúlog din akó kahit na maingay.

blocks.title: Remember
items: A participle describes a noun or pronoun, like an adjective.
Tagalog participles: **naka- + root word** (a noun or a verb).
They show a **state, condition or appearance**: nakaupô, nakatayô, nakasapatos.
Do not confuse them with the past tense of **maka-** verbs, which show ability (Lesson 18).

vocab.note: Ang batà ay nakaupô sa mataás na sílya = The child is seated on a high chair.
Printed with the ligature -ng: táong nakasalamíng iyón (that man with eyeglasses).

exercises.q: How does a participle work in a sentence?
options: Like an adjective: it describes a noun or pronoun
exercises.answer: Like an adjective: it describes a noun or pronoun
exercises.explain: A gerund works like a noun; a participle works like an adjective.

exercises.q: How is a Tagalog participle formed?
exercises.explain: Pag- makes gerunds (Lesson 38); naka- makes participles.

exercises.q: What kind of root can take naka-?
exercises.explain: nakaupô (from a verb root), nakasapatos (from a noun).

exercises.q: What does a naka- participle express?
options: The state, condition or appearance of a person or thing
exercises.answer: The state, condition or appearance of a person or thing
exercises.explain: Ability is shown by maka- verbs (Lesson 18).

exercises.q: How many tense forms does a naka- participle have?
exercises.explain: It is descriptive, just like an adjective.

exercises.q: The past tense of a maka- verb shows…
exercises.explain: Maka- verbs are purely action words (Lesson 18).

exercises.q: In Lesson 18, what did nakatúlog mean?
exercises.explain: Nakatúlog is the past tense of the maka- verb makatúlog.

exercises.q: What does nakaupô mean in "Ang batà ay nakaupô sa mataás na sílya"?
exercises.explain: The child is seated on a high chair.
Nakatayô sa tabí ng pintô ang áking iná = My mother is standing by the door.

exercises.q: "Silá ay nakakotse nang dumatíng." What does it mean?
options: They were in a car when they arrived.
They were able to buy a car.
exercises.answer: They were in a car when they arrived.

exercises.explain: Dápat nakamaóng ka = you should be in jeans.

exercises.q: "Bulág ang táong nakasalamíng iyón." What does nakasalamíng describe?
options: the man, who has eyeglasses on
exercises.answer: the man, who has eyeglasses on
exercises.explain: That man with eyeglasses is blind.

exercises.q: In "Kailángang nakasapatos ang batà sa paglalarô", which word is a gerund (Lesson 38)?
exercises.explain: Paglalarô (playing) comes from maglarô; nakasapatos is a participle.
Nakatulalâ si Miriam = Miriam is in shock.

Match gerund or participle to its job.

recap: A participle describes a noun or pronoun, like an adjective; a gerund works like a noun.
Tagalog participles are naka- + a root word, which can be a noun or a verb.
They show a state, condition or appearance: nakaupô (seated), nakasapatos (in shoes), nakakotse (in a car).
Naka- participles have no tense forms.
Do not confuse them with the past tense of maka- verbs, which show ability (nakatúlog = was able to sleep).
